props.title: Contempt
props.initialSlug: Marriage crumbles amid film industry tensions

sections.content: Contempt (1963) stands as Jean-Luc Godard's most direct commentary on commercial filmmaking, using CinemaScope and vivid color to deconstruct both Hollywood and crumbling relationships. Set against the backdrop of a troubled adaptation of Homer's Odyssey, the film stars Michel Piccoli as a screenwriter and Brigitte Bardot as his wife, whose marriage disintegrates during a fateful production in Capri. Godard deliberately contrasts Georges Delerue's sweeping orchestral score with clinical observations of domestic strife, creating an unsettling meditation on art versus commerce. The film's influence echoes through later works like 8½ (1963) and Day for Night (1973), establishing a template for meta-commentary on filmmaking itself.

sections.content: The film's architectural elements, particularly Casa Malaparte perched on Capri's cliffs, serve as a modernist stage for ancient themes. Godard's camera treats the location like another character, with long tracking shots that echo the emotional distance between characters. This approach influenced later films about filmmaking like The Player (1992) and Adaptation (2002), where physical spaces reflect creative and personal conflicts. Raoul Coutard's cinematography, especially in the apartment sequence, creates a claustrophobic atmosphere that would inspire generations of New Wave directors.

The film's treatment of translation and miscommunication - with characters speaking French, English, German, and Italian - creates a Tower of Babel effect that mirrors the fragmentation of modern relationships. This multilingual approach influenced later works like Lost in Translation (2003) and Certified Copy (2010), where language barriers serve as metaphors for emotional disconnection. Fritz Lang's presence as himself adds another layer of meta-commentary, bridging Hollywood's golden age with European art cinema. SUBHEAD: The Influence on Modern Cinema

sections.content: Godard's deconstruction of classical cinema techniques in Contempt reverberates through contemporary filmmaking. Directors like Olivier Assayas in Clouds of Sils Maria (2014) and Quentin Tarantino in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) have drawn from Contempt's playbook of examining the film industry's transformation. The famous opening sequence, with its extended bed conversation between Bardot and Piccoli, has been referenced countless times, notably in Le Mépris: The Story of a Film (2009) and Jean-Luc Godard's own later works.
